stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.07", Sentence = "NPR analysis 3.5 years post-an,bio,c exposure in a clusterrandomised trial of mass-azithromycin administra,on showed a trend toward decreased NPR diversity (p = 0.07) in azithromycin clusters when compared to placebo clusters, with just 25 samples per group (unpublished data)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: An,microbial resistance (AMR) to first line an,bio,cs for pneumonia is a major global health problem, and AMR-adributable deaths are prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa.
Improved data on how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource limited se]ngs is crucial.
The nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their resistome, the gene,c determinants of AMR.
No study has explored whether human resistome composi,on in children with pneumonia is associated with health outcomes.

This study will examine whether an,bio,c treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired nasopharyngeal resistome in children, and whether this is associated with re-hospitalisa,on.

This is an observa,onal case-control study, that will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months from four groups in Blantyre, Malawi: healthy children in the community (healthy community), children with pneumonia treated in the community (community pneumonia), NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
children hospitalised with pneumonia (hospital pneumonia) and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia (re-hospitalised pneumonia).

Nasopharyngeal swabs will be taken at recruitment and 3-month follow-up study visits for metagenomic sequencing to characterise the nasopharyngeal microbiome and resistome; urine samples will be taken at recruitment for an an,bio,c ac,vity bioassay.
Socio-demographic data, co-morbidi,es, pneumonia severity, an,bio,c exposure and health outcomes will be recorded.
Cross-sec,onal comparisons between groups at recruitment will examine whether nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) composi,on differs by pneumonia severity, an,bio,c and healthcare exposure.
Longitudinal comparisons within groups will assess the dynamics of NPR composi,on over ,me.
The study is powered to detect a medium effect size (Cohen's D = 0.505) change in the rela,ve abundance of an,bio,c resistance genes (ARGs) between all four groups.
Primary outcomes are the difference in beta diversity (Bray-Cur,s dissimilarity index), and rela,ve abundance of ARG classes in the NPR.

The primary objec,ves are to es,mate the difference in diversity and rela,ve abundance of the NPR between hospitalised pneumonia par,cipants when compared to 1) healthy community and 2) community pneumonia par,cipants, and to inves,gate whether par,cipants re-hospitalised with pneumonia within a 3-month period have a persistent hospital-acquired NPR padern.

The study has been approved by the Kamuzu University of Heath Sciences Research Ethics Commidee (KUREC, formerly Malawi College of Medicine Research Ethics Commidee; Ref: P.10/24-1200) and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Commidee (LSTM REC; Ref: 24-076).

text.text: Our study aims to answer the following research ques,on: does an,bio,c treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired NPR in Malawian children, and is this associated with adverse health outcomes in a resource-limited se]ng?

This is an observa,onal case-control study with a cohort component to assess the evolu,on of the NPR under selec,ve pressure of an,bio,c use and hospital admission for pneumonia in children aged 12-36 months in Malawi.
The study will describe the impact of an,bio,c selec,ve pressure and exposure to the hospital environment on the NPR of Malawian children with pneumonia.

The study will also inves,gate the hypothesis that a hospital-acquired NPR is associated with adverse health outcomes following discharge, by examining whether NPR composi,on is associated with hospital readmission.

This study will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months in four groups: healthy children in the community, children with pneumonia managed in the community, children hospitalised with pneumonia, and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia.

For the healthy community group, 83 healthy children will be recruited from Ndirande Township using established recruitment protocols for pneumococcal carriage surveys (18); random number genera,on will be used to select the health surveillance assistant (HSA) catchment areas on a pre-defined map of Ndirande.

text.text: In total, the study aims to recruit 350 study par,cipants: 83 healthy community par,cipants, 92 community pneumonia par,cipants, 92 hospital pneumonia par,cipants and 83 re-hospitalised pneumonia par,cipants.
Study groups with a sample size of 92 par,cipants permit a 10% loss to follow-up.

Hospitalised pneumonia par,cipants re-admided to hospital within 3months post-recruitment will be excluded from the control group in the case-control analysis.
Con,nuous variables will be summarised by means and SD, or medians and IQR if the distribu,on exhibits skew.

Differences in incidence of adverse health outcomes will be compared across study groups using the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test.

Primary endpoint analyses will only include par,cipants with complete follow-up data.
Analyses for secondary and exploratory outcomes will include all par,cipants.
